title: No, diplomas are not a substitute for learning
author: Kelsey Piper
summary: In The Argument's Worst Take of the Week column, Kelsey Piper takes aim at Miriam Pawel's New York Times op-ed urging the University of California Regents to resist faculty calls to restore the SAT. Piper argues that Pawel's defense, that UC students may struggle with basic math but are graduating at record rates, confuses granting credentials with building capabilities. If students are less capable yet graduating more often, she reasons, standards are being lowered, and employers will stop treating UC degrees as evidence of competence. That would destroy the very economic mobility Pawel invokes, since UC degrees have lifted students by signaling rigorous preparation. Piper points out that California's 1960 Master Plan already guarantees broad access through community colleges and Cal State, with a strong transfer pathway into the UC system, so there is no need to lower standards at the top.
points: Piper frames Pawel's argument as the straw-man view that handing out degrees is success even when students cannot do math.
Some UC students admitted without test scores struggled in middle school remedial classes and could not add fractions.
A degree that no longer signals competence, she argues, stops functioning as an engine of economic mobility.
California's Master Plan offers free or low-cost access through community colleges and Cal State schools.
Nearly one-third of entering UC students are transfers, 94 percent of them from community colleges.
quotes: If I were to come up with a straw man caricature of the worst imaginable progressive ideas on education, it would sound something like this: “Sure, our kids can’t do basic math. But a successful education system isn’t one that teaches math. It’s one that hands out degrees to everyone. We are handing out more degrees than ever, so we’re succeeding.

If students at UC schools are less capable than ever but graduating at higher rates than ever, the obvious conclusion is that standards are being lowered in order to achieve the desired graduation rates.

If you extrapolate this situation — with no test for academic readiness at admission and pressure to graduate everyone admitted — there will ultimately be no reason to believe a graduate of a UC school is any more qualified for a job than a person who never went to college.
If degrees cease to communicate those things, then the UCs will no longer be engines of economic mobility at all.

We can offer education to everybody without locking anyone into a prescribed path and without lowering standards at top schools — and we know that this can be done because we’ve been successfully doing it for decades!

The only thing wrong with it is that a few misguided ideologues think that UC Berkeley and UC San Diego can provide a world-class education competitive with any Ivy League school even if their admitted students are not prepared to do any of the coursework. But they cannot.
